A railway gate on the railway line that crosses Mavelikkara- Kayamkulam Road at Kakkanad situated between Cheppadu and Kayamkulam Railway Stations, needs to be frequently closed due to the passing trains and as this road experiences heavy vehicular traffic.

sentences.text: The frequent closures of the gate cause serious disruption to the vehicular traffic and inconvenience to the public.
In 1992, the Government of Kerala decided to construct a Road Over Bridge at this place.
But even after thirty years since then, the project is still at a stage of determining what the alignment should be for this Road Over Bridge.
This position has arisen because of the litigation instituted by the residents on either side of the road where the project is proposed to be constructed, questioning the alignment.
2. The Petitioner No.1 had earlier filed W.P.(C) No.23099 of 2021.

Pursuant to a notification issued for acquiring an extent of around 0.298 hectares of land for the construction of the Road Over Bridge, Respondent No. 2 conducted a Social Impact Assessment Study and submitted a report on 18 November 2022 (Exhibit-P3).
The Petitioners filed W.P.(C) No.41009 of 2022, challenging Exhibit-P3 Study on the ground that the feasibility of an alternative proposal was not considered.

The learned Single Judge, by judgment dated 13 June 2023, disposed of the Writ Petition, directing Respondent No. 2 to prepare an additional report considering the alternative site proposed by the Petitioners.

Thereafter, a further study was conducted by Respondent No. 2 regarding the alternative site suggested by the Petitioners and submitted Exhibit-P8, an additional report, opining that the alternative site is not feasible and viable.

Exhibit-P8 was placed before the Expert Committee as per Sections 7(2) and 7(3) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (Act of 2013).

sentences.text: The Expert Committee accepted Exhibit-P8 report and decided to make a recommendation to the District Collector to proceed further in terms of the original proposal.
Exhibit-P7 decision and Exhibit- P8 report were challenged by the Petitioners by filing W.P.(C) No.5224 of 2024.
This Writ Petition was dismissed by the learned Single Judge by judgment dated 12 August 2024.
Challenging this judgment, the Petitioners have filed this Writ Appeal under Section 5 of the Kerala High Court Act.

4. We have heard Mr. R. Rajasekharan Pillai, learned counsel for the Appellants/Petitioners, Mr. A.
Dinesh Rao, learned Standing Counsel for Respondent No.1, and Mr. Sukumar Nainan Oommen,
learned counsel for Respondent No.2.

sentences.text: The primary ground for the challenge by the Petitioners is that the Social Impact Assessment Study has not been carried out as contemplated under the provisions of the Act of 2013.
It is contended that the alternative site suggested by the Petitioners is more viable and practical, and it is not necessary to implement the project as per the original plan.
It is also contended that in the Right to Information Act, 2005, Respondent No.2 has accepted that there has been no Social Impact Assessment Study 2024:KER:94320 conducted.
It is submitted that the decision of the learned Single Judge in W.P.(C) No. 41009 of 2022 mandated the Respondents to carry out a fresh Social Impact Assessment Study, which has not been done.
Therefore, the reports will have to be quashed and set aside, and a Social Impact Assessment Study needs to be conducted.
6. We find no merit in the contentions of the Petitioners and hold that the learned Single Judge was not in error in dismissing the Petition for the following reasons.
7. Chapter II of the Act of 2013 deals with the Determination of Social Impact and Public Purpose.
Section 4 therein specifies the Preparation of the Social Impact Assessment Study.
Thereafter, a public hearing is conducted under Section 5, leading to the Publication of the Social Impact Assessment Study as per Section 6.
The Social Impact Assessment Report is then evaluated by an independent multi-disciplinary Expert Group under Section 7 of the Act of 2013.

Rule 7 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation, and Resettlement (Social Impact Assessment and Consent) Rules, 2014 (Rule of 2014) lays down the Process of Conducting the Social Impact Assessment.

sentences.text:
The Social Impact Assessment Team has to consider and analyze various parameters, which include the parameter specified under sub-Rule (3) Clause (d) -
possible alternative sites for the project and their feasibility.
It is this Rule that has been emphasized by the Petitioners.

8. The learned Single Judge, while disposing of the earlier W.P.(C) No.41009 of 2022, opined in the judgment dated 13 June 2023 that 2024:KER:94320 Exhibit-P3 Social Impact Assessment Study did not suggest that any alternative proposal had been considered.
The learned Single Judge noted the Petitioners' case that such an alternative proposal was mooted at the time of the public hearing.
Therefore, while disposing of W.P.(C) No.41009 of 2022, the learned Single Judge directed Respondent No.2 to prepare an additional report as part of the Social Impact Assessment Study.

In the judgment dated 13 June 2023, the learned Single Judge did not set aside Exhibit-P3 Social Impact Assessment Report but specifically directed for an additional report to be included as part of the original Exhibit-P3 report.

While directing Respondent No.2 to consider the viability of the alternative site, the learned Single Judge made it clear that no opinion on the merits of the Petitioners' claim that the alternative site is more convenient was being expressed.
Therefore, the Petitioners' contention that the learned Single Judge, in the judgment dated 13 June 2023, directed that a fresh Social Impact Assessment Study be carried out is not correct.
It was Respondent No.2 who was specifically directed to file an additional report.
9. The Respondent No. 2 - Centre for Management Development carried out a fresh study.
The proposal submitted for an alternative site was considered, and a report was prepared.

The report states that a representative of Respondent No.2 visited the project site along with officials from the Revenue Department and the Kerala Rail Development Corporation Limited and had discussions Rajesh K vs The Managing Director on 9 December, 2024

The team found that the alternative site proposed by the Petitioners is located around 50 metres away from the existing road.
Most of the proposed area consists of 2024:KER:94320 agricultural land with wetland features.
The team observed that the alternative would require more land and affect houses and commercial establishments.

Additionally, the alignment proposed by the Petitioners goes through an area fully owned by private parties, necessitating more land acquisition by the Government compared to the previously proposed road.
10. The Report submitted by Respondent No.2 concluded that the alternative proposal promoted by the Petitioners posed challenges.
It would require acquiring a larger area of land, approximately 70 Acres, which was more than three times what the existing proposal necessitates.

It was stated that since the land is paddy land and has the nature of wetlands, issues related to the Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act, 2008 may arise and lead to the wastage of the available Government land as per the original proposal.

sentences.text: It was noted that the Petitioners' proposal would entail creating an additional junction and will have reverse curves in the road alignment.
It will affect residential and commercial structures.
The Report stated that the original proposal does not have these issues and provides a smoother alignment with minimal land acquisition.
The Report further noted that the existing proposal is more economical and technically viable than the alternative.
The Study concluded that considering the originally proposed Road Over Bridge alignment would be an effective and feasible proposal.
It was stated that this conclusion is also backed by its operational efficiency, minimal land requirements, chances of displacements, and adherence to the land acquisition law.
This Report annexed various photographs to demonstrate how the proposal is not viable.

Therefore, the Petitioners' alternative proposal was duly considered by both the study group and the Expert Committee and, for the above reasons, has not been considered viable.
This is not a case where no alternative proposal has been considered or rejected without reason.
The study group and the Expert Committee have applied their minds and found that the proposal for an alternative site is not viable.
The requirements of the Act of 2013 and the Rule of 2014 have been duly complied with.
The information stated to be supplied under the Right to Information Act, therefore, has no relevance.
14. Also, the scope of jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India has to be kept in mind.
The exercise of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is subject to certain well recognized parameters, particularly regarding issues like the alignment of roads.
The High Court, exercising its writ jurisdiction, will not act as an appellate authority over technical and specialized matters.
In the exercise of certiorari jurisdiction in such matters, the focus of judicial review is not on the correctness of the decision but on the decision-making process.

The Court examines whether the process adopted by the decision-making authority complies with the principles of natural justice, is free from arbitrariness, and does not suffer from procedural irregularities or illegality.
In the present case, the decision regarding the alignment of the road has 2024:KER:94320 undergone scrutiny by experts at two levels.

All relevant technical, environmental,
and logistical parameters have been considered.
No further interference in writ jurisdiction is warranted.
15. The project, which is of urgent public utility to alleviate the day- to-day difficulties of the local commuters, which has been pending for more than 30 years, has to be taken forward.
16. The Appeal is dismissed.

A railway gate on the railway line that crosses Mavelikkara- Kayamkulam Road at Kakkanad situated between Cheppadu and Kayamkulam Railway Stations, needs to be frequently closed due to the passing trains and as this road experiences heavy vehicular traffic.
The frequent closures of the gate cause serious disruption to the vehicular traffic and inconvenience to the public.
opennyai_summary.facts:
In 1992, the Government of Kerala decided to construct a Road Over Bridge at this place.
Pursuant to a notification issued for acquiring an extent of around 0.298 hectares of land for the construction of the Road Over Bridge, Respondent No. 2 conducted a Social Impact Assessment Study and submitted a report on 18 November 2022 (Exhibit-P3).
The Petitioners filed W.P.(C) No.41009 of 2022, challenging Exhibit-P3 Study on the ground that the feasibility of an alternative proposal was not considered.
The learned Single Judge, by judgment dated 13 June 2023, disposed of the Writ Petition, directing Respondent No. 2 to prepare an additional report considering the alternative site proposed by the Petitioners.
Exhibit-P8 was placed before the Expert Committee as per Sections 7(2) and 7(3) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (Act of 2013).
The Expert Committee accepted Exhibit-P8 report and decided to make a recommendation to the District Collector to proceed further in terms of the original proposal.
Exhibit-P7 decision and Exhibit- P8 report were challenged by the Petitioners by filing W.P.(C) No.5224 of 2024.
This Writ Petition was dismissed by the learned Single Judge by judgment dated 12 August 2024.
Challenging this judgment, the Petitioners have filed this Writ Appeal under Section 5 of the Kerala High Court Act.
Therefore, while disposing of W.P.(C) No.41009 of 2022, the learned Single Judge directed Respondent No.2 to prepare an additional report as part of the Social Impact Assessment Study.
opennyai_summary.arguments: The primary ground for the challenge by the Petitioners is that the Social Impact Assessment Study has not been carried out as contemplated under the provisions of the Act of 2013.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:

The requirements of the Act of 2013 and the Rule of 2014 have been duly complied with.

14. Also, the scope of jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India has to be kept in mind.
The exercise of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is subject to certain well recognized parameters, particularly regarding issues like the alignment of roads.
The High Court, exercising its writ jurisdiction, will not act as an appellate authority over technical and specialized matters.
In the exercise of certiorari jurisdiction in such matters, the focus of judicial review is not on the correctness of the decision but on the decision-making process.
The Court examines whether the process adopted by the decision-making authority complies with the principles of natural justice, is free from arbitrariness, and does not suffer from procedural irregularities or illegality.
